learning: The NMP (Notes and Multipitch) model from Bittner et al. (Spotify) achieves state-of-the-art results on GuitarSet while outperforming a recent strong instrument-agnostic baseline across multiple datasets, though it does not outperform instrument-specific models for piano and vocals.
supporting_quote: When compared with instrument-specific models, we see that NMP achieves state-of-the-art results on GuitarSet. It however did not outperform the instrument-specific models for piano and vocals.
query: Spotify Basic Pitch GuitarSet transcription accuracy study
research_goal:
Goal: retrieve empirical accuracy figures and evaluation conditions for automatic transcription systems applied to guitar (polyphonic and monophonic), with emphasis on concrete numbers (note F‑measure, onset tolerance windows, pitch MAE/Hz, voicing accuracy, tablature alignment accuracy) reported for Spotify Basic Pitch, GuitarSet and comparable datasets. Also surface robustness tests that vary SNR, backing‑track bleed, chordal density, playing techniques (strummed chords, fingerstyle, bends), microphone/recording quality and tuning deviations.
How to advance research after results are collected: (1) Normalize reported metrics by common tolerances (e.g., 25 ms / 50 ms onset tolerances) and produce a cross‑dataset comparison table showing model, dataset, polyphony level, reported metrics and exact evaluation protocol. (2) Where possible re-run or re-evaluate top SOTA models on GuitarSet and on curated degraded versions (synthetic bleed, reverberation, compression) to estimate real‑world robustness and report degradation curves (accuracy vs SNR, vs bleed ratio). (3) Propose standardized benchmark protocols: fixed onset tolerances, pitch error thresholds, voicing definitions, tablature matching criteria and test splits that include backing tracks.
Additional research directions and concrete experiments: create controlled perturbation experiments (inject backing track bleed at defined dB ratios, add realistic compression/distortion, vary mic distance) to map failure regions; evaluate polyphonic chord recognition separately from single‑note estimation; measure transcription error types (substitution, deletion, insertion) and perceptual impact (which errors matter for learning). Explore multimodal transcription (audio + video/hand pose) for technique‑sensitive errors, and investigate transfer learning from large weakly labeled datasets. If re‑training is feasible, test adversarial robustness and domain adaptation from studio to home recording conditions.

learning: Spotify's Basic Pitch is an open-source, instrument-agnostic, polyphonic audio-to-MIDI transcription library intended to be lightweight and fast while supporting multipitch outputs and pitch-bend detection.
source_title: GitHub - spotify/basic-pitch: A lightweight yet powerful audio-to-MIDI ...
supporting_quote:
Basic Pitch is a Python library for Automatic Music Transcription (AMT), using lightweight neural network developed by [Spotify's Audio Intelligence Lab]. It's small, easy-to-use, `pip install`-able and `npm install`-able via its [sibling repo](https://github.com/spotify/basic-pitch-ts).

Basic Pitch may be simple, but it's is far from "basic"! `basic-pitch` is efficient and easy to use, and its multipitch support, its ability to generalize across instruments, and its note accuracy competes with much larger and more resource-hungry AMT systems.

learning: In a Guitar-focused end-to-end pipeline (Fretwork), combining GuitarSet with the large DadaGP tab dataset and a transformer sequence model increased full-pipeline F1 from ~0.42 (greedy) to 0.77, and the authors identify pitch-detection (Spotify Basic Pitch) as the main bottleneck.
source_title: Fretwork: An Open-Source Music Intelligence Platform for Guitarists
supporting_quote: Starting from a baseline of ~0.42 full-pipeline F1 with a greedy algorithm that evaluates each note independently, our CAGED + voicing algorithm reached 0.54. Adding the DadaGP position prior pushed this to 0.72, and a transformer sequence model trained on DadaGP brought the final result to 0.77. The near-match F1 of 0.78 reveals that the fretboard assignment itself is largely correct; the main bottleneck is pitch detection, for which we are constrained by Spotify's Basic Pitch pitch detection algorithm.

learning: In a randomized trial with beginner violinists using the TELMI SkyNote system, real-time visual feedback (RTVF) improved bowing kinematics during practice but degraded sound quality while feedback was present; however, at retention the feedback group showed better sound-quality outcomes, particularly in control of sound dynamics.
source_title: Real-time sound and motion feedback for violin bow technique learning: A controlled, randomized trial
supporting_quote: At the practice phase, the experimental group improved their bowing kinematics in comparison to the control group, but this was at the expense of impairing the sound quality of their performance. At the retention phase, the experimental group showed better results in sound quality, especially concerning control of sound dynamics.
query: automated feedback music learning retention transfer randomized trial review
research_goal:
Goal: collect randomized trials, longitudinal studies and systematic reviews that test whether automated feedback (apps, algorithmic scoring, AI tutors), video/audio self‑review, or computer feedback produce measurable improvements in independent performance, retention (delayed tests) and transfer to unfamiliar material or ensemble contexts. Include named empirical studies cited in the brief (e.g., Boucher, Creech & Dubé on video feedback for classical guitarists), AI guitar assistant research such as 'Ground truths' 2025, and any null or negative results.
How to advance research after reviewing the literature: (1) Critically appraise study designs (sample sizes, randomization, active vs passive controls, masking of evaluators, retention intervals, transfer tasks) and extract effect sizes for performance, retention and transfer outcomes. (2) Identify mediators and moderators (learner level, practice dose, feedback specificity, feedback frequency, adaptive personalization) that predict whether automated feedback helps or creates dependency. (3) Synthesize counterevidence: catalog studies showing no benefit or detrimental effects (overreliance on scores, reduced autonomy) and analyze methodological reasons (short interventions, in‑app outcomes only).
Additional experimental recommendations: design a preregistered RCT with plateaued adult intermediate guitarists comparing (a) adaptive automated feedback, (b) human teacher feedback, (c) video self‑review with guided rubrics, (d) combined automated+human, and (e) active control (practice without feedback). Measure immediate learning, delayed retention (1–3 months), and transfer to novel pieces and cold ensemble playing. Include blinded expert ratings, objective feature measures and learner motivation metrics. Also test feedback withdrawal (wean participants off feedback) to detect dependency. Where possible, instrument sessions (audio+video+IMU) to link specific feedback types to measurable skill gains.

learning: Across seven RCTs (125 medical-student participants) comparing VR simulators with haptic feedback versus box trainers (BT) for laparoscopic skills, box trainers produced a superior learning curve and greater improvements across more performance parameters, while there was no significant difference between VR and BT for transfer to surgical environments.
source_title: Comparing Learning Outcomes of Virtual Reality (VR) Simulators Using Haptic Feedback Versus Box Trainer (BT) in Laparoscopic Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
supporting_quote: Results indicated that BTs demonstrated a superior learning curve, with participants achieving proficiency faster than those using VR. Both simulators showed significant learning effects; however, BTs resulted in greater improvements across more performance parameters. Regarding skill transfer to surgical environments, there was no significant difference between the two groups, suggesting both approaches effectively support surgical skill transfer.

learning: On open-ended (OE) constructed-response items the two automated raters (ChatGPT‑4 and Gemini) showed higher pairwise agreement than the two human raters: Robinson’s A = 0.71 for AI–AI vs 0.67 for human–human, and Gwet’s AC2 = 0.82 for AI–AI vs 0.43 for human–human (study used 46 OE responses, 4 raters).
source_title: Bridging minds and machines: a comparative study of AI and human rater ...
supporting_quote: According to Robinson’s A, the highest level of agreement is observed between the two automated raters (0.71), while the lowest occurs between Rater-1 and GPT (0.61). Notably, the agreement between the two human raters (0.67) is lower than that between the two automated raters (0.71). Similarly, Gwet’s AC2 values indicate that the highest agreement is again between the two automated raters (0.82), whereas the lowest agreement is observed between GPT and Rater 2 (0.30). As with Robinson’s A, the agreement between the automated raters (0.82) exceeds that of the human raters (0.43).
query: automated performance assessment expert raters agreement study
research_goal:
Goal: assemble studies that quantify agreement between automated performance‑assessment systems and human expert raters (correlations, ICCs, Cohen’s kappa where applicable) across dimensions including timing/rhythm, intonation, technique, and expressiveness. Also collect literature on human rubric reliability (consensual assessment technique, collegiate jazz improvisation rubrics) to define target criterion reliability for automated systems.
How to advance research after obtaining findings: (1) Create an evaluation matrix that maps automated feature outputs (e.g., timing deviation distributions, intonation cent deviation, articulation metrics) to human rubric items and reports effect sizes and r or ICC values for each mapping. (2) Identify systematic failure modes (low correlation for expressiveness, genre dependence, bias toward vibrato/steady tempo) and produce an error taxonomy. (3) Recommend minimum human benchmark: for an automated metric to be 'acceptable' it should approach inter‑rater agreement (e.g., automated-human correlation >= average human–human ICC for that rubric). Implement calibration procedures (linear scaling, IRT) to align automated scores to rater distributions.
Additional research possibilities: design multi‑rater validation studies with 4–8 expert raters, blinded and using standardized rubrics, and compare automated scores across subgroups (genre, age, level). Use mixed‑effects models to separate rater variance, performer variance, and method variance. Investigate methods for automated systems to express uncertainty (confidence intervals) and to flag ambiguous cases for human review. Explore interpretable features and counterfactual explanations (e.g., show which notes/times drove a low score) to support teacher acceptance and troubleshooting.

learning: In surgical-simulation research, automated/AI assessment systems often reach very high accuracy on structured motor tasks (examples: Sugiyama et al. AUC 0.85–1.00; Prevezanou et al. 97–99% accuracy on LAP Mentor VR with ML+LSTM; Pan et al. 84.8–92.04% for da Vinci suturing), but the literature shows large methodological heterogeneity and reporting gaps that limit generalisability across tasks and contexts.
source_title: Automated and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Derived Performance ...
supporting_quote: Overall metrics of accuracy: Overall accuracy is a primary measure of AI performance relative to expert or gold-standard benchmarks. Sugiyama et al. [18] reported AUC values of 0.85-1.00 for identifying gestures during end-to-side anastomosis, indicating near-perfect discrimination for some tasks. Prevezanou et al. [20] attained 97-99% accuracy using seven machine learning models combined with LSTM, where the strength of temporal models in predicting skill acquisition from VR laparoscopic simulation is highlighted. Pan et al. [22] reported task classification accuracies ranging from 84.8% to 92.04% for da Vinci suturing tasks, demonstrating that CNN-based vision models can replace traditional sensors without compromising precision.

query: NMP Basic Pitch GuitarSet F-measure
research_goal:
Goal: retrieve authoritative, per-paper/per-dataset numeric transcription metrics reported for Spotify NMP/Basic Pitch and close SOTA models on guitar-focused and general multipitch datasets (GuitarSet, MAESTRO, Slakh, Molina, MusicNet, DadaGP where applicable). Specifically collect note-level F (with stated onset/offset tolerances), Fno or onset-only F, frame-level accuracy, pitch MAE (Hz and cents), voicing accuracy, pitch-bend detection rates, and tablature-alignment/edit metrics; capture exact evaluation protocols, sample sizes, train/test splits, and any instrument/polphony breakdowns reported. Flag where metrics are computed with different tolerances (e.g., 25 ms vs 50 ms) or nonstandard voicing definitions.

How to advance research after retrieving results: (1) normalize all collected metrics to a common set of tolerances (propose 25 ms and 50 ms onset tolerances, 50 cents pitch tolerance and per-note pitch MAE) and produce a cross-dataset comparison table showing model, dataset, polyphony level, exact metric definitions and sample sizes. (2) Identify models with open-source checkpoints (Basic Pitch, NMP, Fretwork components) and plan reproducible re-evaluations on canonical splits (GuitarSet test split, MAESTRO v3, Slakh v2) to confirm numbers and extract granular error types (insertions/deletions/substitutions). (3) Define standardized tablature alignment metrics (note-to-string/fret matching, edit-distance F1) and re-run pipeline evaluations where tablature is part of the output. 

Additional research directions and concrete experiments: re-evaluate top models on curated degraded variants (synthetic backing-track bleed, SNR sweep +30 to -6 dB, MP3/AAC compression at 320/128/64 kbps, reverberation RT60 0.2–1.5 s, added harmonic distortion/clipping, tuning offsets ±5–50 cents). Measure transcription degradation curves (accuracy vs SNR/bleed/codec/RT60). Break down errors by technique (strummed chords, fingerstyle, bends, slides, harmonics) using GuitarSet annotations or manual labels. Where re-training is feasible, test domain adaptation strategies (data augmentation, finetuning on degraded mixes, adversarial augmentation) and report improvements. Also evaluate multimodal approaches (audio+video hand-pose) by re-running models with pose features to see whether technique-sensitive errors reduce. Finally, plan perceptual validation: listener studies to determine which error types are consequential for learning tasks and to set task-relevant accuracy targets for an AI tutor (e.g., what F-score corresponds to usable feedback for rhythm vs pitch guidance). Flag speculative items (re-training, multimodal) when evidence is absent.

learning: In run-time/memory benchmarks on a 2017 MacBook Pro, NMP used 490 MB peak memory and 7 s for a short file (and 951 MB / 24 s for a 7m45s Slakh file), while the comparable MI-AMT used 561 MB / 10 s for the short file and 3.3 GB / 96 s for the long file.
source_title: A Lightweight Instrument-Agnostic Model for Polyphonic Note ... - arXiv
supporting_quote: We find that both methods are comparable in estimated overhead, with NMP using 490 MB peak memory and taking 7 s and MI-AMT using 561 MB and taking 10 s; however on the long file, NMP substantially outperforms MI-AMT, using only 951 MB peak memory and taking 24 s, while MI-AMT used 3.3 GB and took 96 s.

query: Basic Pitch robustness study backing-track bleed SNR
research_goal:
Goal: locate peer-reviewed or conference evaluations that quantify how Basic Pitch, NMP and similar instrument-agnostic multipitch systems degrade under realistic distortions — backing-track bleed, low SNR, codec compression, reverberation, mic distance, and tuning deviations. Extract exact degradation experiments: SNR/bleed levels tested, distortion types, evaluation metrics used (note F, frame accuracy, pitch MAE), datasets and sample counts, and whether tests used synthetic mixes or real noisy recordings.

How to advance research after results are found: (1) synthesize a standardized robustness test battery and parameter grid (recommended: SNR sweep +30, +20, +10, 0, -6 dB; bleed ratios 0–50% energy; compression bitrates 320/192/128/64 kbps; RT60 0.2/0.5/1.0/1.5 s; tuning offsets ±5/25/50 cents; distortions: soft clipping 1–6 dB). (2) Implement reproducible experiments: mix clean guitar stems with backing tracks from GuitarSet and DadaGP at target SNRs using measured LUFS or dB SPL, transcode with common codecs, and evaluate models producing accuracy-vs-condition curves. (3) Measure not only aggregate metrics but error-mode breakdown (insertions/deletions/substitutions, chordal vs single-note loss, voicing flips) and create visualizations of failure regions. 

Additional research directions and concrete experiments: (a) Evaluate whether augmenting training data with simulated bleed and codec artifacts or finetuning on small amounts of in-domain noisy audio improves robustness (report sample efficiency). (b) Test domain adaptation and adversarial training to improve worst-case performance; quantify catastrophic failure thresholds. (c) Compare instrument-agnostic models with instrument-specific baselines under the same distortions to see which generalize better to home-recording conditions. (d) Link robustness results to pedagogical utility: run small-scale learning studies where participants receive automated feedback generated under different model accuracy/robustness conditions, then measure transfer and retention on independent performance tasks to identify minimum acceptable model reliability for tutoring. Note speculative steps (user studies and retraining) and prioritize reproducibility (publish scripts, seeds, exact mixing parameters).

learning: Assessment-, generative- and comprehensive/adaptive-AI tools produce different psychological effects in music learning: assessment-oriented AI ‘most consistently strengthened ability beliefs via objectified, visualized feedback’ and oriented cognitive agency to self-monitoring/self-reflectiveness; generative AI ‘tended to enhance value–attitude beliefs and intentionality’; comprehensive/adaptive AI ‘more often supported forethought and sustained engagement’.
source_title: Empowerment or dependency? A systematic review of the impacts ...
supporting_quote: Assessment-oriented AI most consistently strengthened ability beliefs via objectified, visualized feedback and positioned cognitive agency around self-monitoring, self-reactiveness, and self-reflectiveness. Generative AI tended to enhance value–attitude beliefs and intentionality by lowering technical barriers and reconfiguring learners’ creative roles toward aesthetic decision-making and output curation. Comprehensive/Adaptive AI more often supported forethought and sustained engagement by dynamically maintaining alignment between task challenge and learner capability.
query: automated feedback music education systematic review
research_goal:
Goal: locate peer‑reviewed systematic reviews and meta‑analyses that evaluate automated or computerized feedback (apps, algorithmic scoring, AI tutors, audio/video self‑review tools) on music learning outcomes, with emphasis on randomized or longitudinal designs reporting retention (delayed tests) and transfer to new material or ensemble contexts. This will establish the current aggregated evidence base, pooled effect sizes, common outcome measures, and documented limitations or biases across studies. 

How to advance research once results are found: extract effect sizes (Hedges' g) for immediate performance, delayed retention, and transfer outcomes; code study moderators (age, instrument, learner level, sample size, randomization quality, active vs passive control, blinding of raters, retention interval, duration and dose of practice, feedback modality and specificity). Run subgroup analyses or meta‑regressions to identify whether feedback specificity, adaptivity, learner level, or practice dose predict benefit versus harm. Actively search for publication bias and selectively report null results. Use the review to specify minimal methodological standards (sample size targets, blinded expert ratings, retention >1 month, transfer tasks) for confirmatory RCTs. Additional research directions: (1) expand to adjacent domains (speech, motor rehabilitation) for mechanistic insights about feedback dependency and attentional load; (2) compare real‑time vs delayed automated feedback; (3) ask whether observed effects differ by feedback modality (visual score vs audio examples vs haptic), and (4) assess whether automated feedback fosters autonomy or dependency by including feedback‑withdrawal tests in designs.

learning: Deep learning architectures (CNNs + RNNs; Transformers) have materially advanced MIR: CNNs+RNNs ‘effectively process the time–frequency characteristics of musical audio, achieving near-human performance in tasks such as instrument recognition, onset detection, and chord recognition,’ and Transformer/pretrained audio foundation models (e.g., MERT, MusicBERT) provide powerful representations used for downstream assessment and generation.
source_title: Recent advances in artificial intelligence for music education
supporting_quote: The combination of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) [23,41] and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) [42,43] effectively processes the time-frequency characteristics of musical audio, achieving near-human performance in tasks such as instrument recognition, onset detection, and chord recognition.

query: randomized trial automated guitar feedback
research_goal:
Goal: find randomized controlled trials and longitudinal empirical studies that specifically test automated feedback systems (audio scoring apps, AI guitar tutors, algorithmic assessment, guided video self‑review) with guitarists—ideally adult intermediate learners—and that report objective performance outcomes, delayed retention, and transfer (novel pieces, ensemble playing). Prioritize trials that name authors cited in the brief (e.g., Boucher, Creech & Dubé) and newer AI guitar assistant work (e.g., 'Ground truths' 2025), and catalog any null/negative findings. 

How to advance research once results are found: for each trial extract detailed metadata (population age/level, sample size, randomization procedure, control condition type, masking of outcome raters, retention interval, transfer tasks, objective features measured, effect sizes, and reported failure modes). Evaluate risk of bias (selection, performance, detection) and compute pooled effect estimates where possible. Identify whether trials included feedback withdrawal or dependency tests and whether blinded expert ratings matched automated scores. Use findings to design the preregistered RCT proposed in the brief: specify comparator arms (adaptive automated, human teacher, guided video self‑review, combined, active control), sample size powered for small–moderate effects, blinded expert adjudication, retention at 1–3 months, transfer to cold ensemble playing, and instrumentation (audio+video+IMU). Additional directions: search for implementation details of the automated systems (scoring algorithms, thresholds, latency) to assess plausible measurement error sources; seek raw or item‑level scoring data to compute inter‑rater and automated–human agreement; and flag work on attentional load and dual‑task costs for real‑time visual feedback to avoid designs that impair learning while producing in‑session gains.

learning: In the 2019 virtual‑guitar study by Passalenti et al., the combination of vibrotactile and force feedback yielded the most realistic experience and reduced inadvertent string hits, while vibrotactile‑only and force‑only conditions did not differ significantly.

supporting_quote: The results indicate that the combination of vibrotactile and force feedback elicits the most realistic experience, and during this condition, participants were less likely to inadvertently hit strings. Notably, no significant differences were found between the conditions involving either vibrotactile or force feedback.

query: automated music performance assessment ICC study
research_goal:
Goal: locate empirical studies that quantify agreement between automated music-performance assessment systems and human expert raters (reporting Pearson r, ICC, Cohen’s kappa, Gwet’s AC, Bland–Altman, or other agreement indices) across dimensions such as timing/rhythm, intonation, technique, and expressiveness. Emphasize adult or adult-like populations (guitar, classical/folk guitar, piano, voice, violin, saxophone) and studies that use standardized rubrics (consensual assessment technique, collegiate jazz improvisation rubrics, or itemized performance rubrics). Extract sample sizes, number of raters, rater expertise, rubric items, scoring scales, study design (cross‑sectional, longitudinal, blinded), and whether results report delayed retention or transfer.

How to advance research after obtaining results: (1) Build an evaluation matrix mapping automated feature outputs (e.g., timing deviation distributions, IOI variability, cent deviation, spectral centroid/articulation proxies, string/bending/vibrato detectors) to rubric items; for each mapping report effect sizes and r or ICC between automated metric and human rubric score. (2) Estimate target acceptance thresholds by computing average human–human ICC per rubric item and define automated acceptability as automated–human correlation or ICC approaching that average. (3) Use mixed‑effects models or Generalizability Theory to partition variance into performer, rater, and method components; estimate how much method (automated) variance inflates or reduces total error. (4) Design multi‑rater validation studies (4–8 expert raters) with 50–200 recorded performances stratified by genre/level; pre‑register analysis plan, use blinded ratings, compute ICC(2,k), Bland–Altman plots, and bootstrap CIs for agreement metrics. (5) Implement calibration procedures (linear scaling, item response theory, or Bayesian hierarchical alignment) to align automated outputs to rater distributions; validate on held‑out performances and report calibrated uncertainty (confidence intervals) and flagging thresholds for human review.

Additional directions: test automated reliability across subgroups (genre, recording quality, performer level), evaluate interpretability methods (feature attributions, score decompositions, counterfactual suggestions identifying notes/times driving low scores), and examine human trust/acceptance via mixed‑methods teacher evaluations. Consider adversarial and failure‑mode probing (e.g., vibrato-heavy passages, rubato, ornamentation, backing‑track bleed) and quantify systematic biases (genre or technique preference). For statistics, plan Bayesian hierarchical models to estimate posterior distributions of agreement metrics and decision rules for when to defer to human raters.

learning: Fretwork (UC Berkeley MIDS capstone) evaluated on GuitarSet (LOOCV) and reported full-pipeline playable-tab F1 improving from ~0.42 (greedy) → 0.54 (CAGED+voicing) → 0.72 (+DadaGP) → 0.77 (transformer); near‑match F1 0.78; authors state the main bottleneck is pitch detection (not their fretboard assignment).
source_title: Fretwork: An Open-Source Music Intelligence Platform for Guitarists
supporting_quote: Starting from a baseline of ~0.42 full-pipeline F1 with a greedy algorithm that evaluates each note independently, our CAGED + voicing algorithm reached 0.54. Adding the DadaGP position prior pushed this to 0.72, and a transformer sequence model trained on DadaGP brought the final result to 0.77. The near-match F1 of 0.78 reveals that the fretboard assignment itself is largely correct; the main bottleneck is pitch detection, not our algorithm.
query: GuitarSet Spotify Basic Pitch transcription benchmarks
research_goal:
Goal: compile benchmark accuracy figures for polyphonic guitar transcription, onset detection, and tablature extraction on standard MIR datasets (GuitarSet, IRMAS where relevant, MusicNet, MAPS, and Spotify Basic Pitch/Pop datasets). Focus on reported metrics such as note F‑measure, onset/offset F1, onset tolerance windows, pitch‑class accuracy, transcription frame F1, and tablature/string/fret accuracy; include conditions that simulate realistic practice settings (backing‑track bleed, SNR levels, smartphone recordings, compression). Extract model types evaluated (classical signal processing, NMF, CRNN, Transformer, Basic Pitch/Onsets and Frames extensions), training data, and any reported degradation under noise/bleed (quantify performance drop per SNR or bleed percentage).

How to advance research after obtaining results: (1) Create a transparent benchmark table showing best‑reported numbers and experimental conditions (dataset split, polyphony, mixed‑audio bleed, mic type). (2) Define standardized robustness tests: SNR sweep (e.g., +20 to -10 dB), simulated backing‑track bleed levels, MP3/AAC compression, room reverberation; report metric decay curves so practitioners can anticipate real‑world performance. (3) Produce an error taxonomy for guitar transcription (missed fretted-note detection due to bending/vibrato, note splitting from distortion, false positives from backing tracks, string misassignment in tablature) and map these to downstream assessment risks (e.g., rhythm score misestimation vs. pitch‑based expressiveness misclassification). (4) Recommend augmentation/finetuning strategies (mixing dry guitar with real backing tracks, adversarial bleed examples, multi‑mic training) and evaluation protocols (holdout recordings recorded on smartphones/USB interfaces to measure generalization).

Additional directions: investigate how transcription uncertainty propagates into automated assessment metrics (propagate note onset/pitch confidence into score CIs), explore hybrid approaches using multi‑modal inputs (audio+video for fingering detection) to improve tablature extraction, and propose community benchmarks for ‘practice‑condition’ transcription with a shared corpus of smartphone recordings and backing tracks. Consider evaluation of Spotify Basic Pitch extensions and replicate top results with public code to verify reproducibility; where gaps exist, recommend replication studies under varied recording conditions.

learning: NMP (Bittner et al., ICASSP 2022) is a low-resource, instrument-agnostic polyphonic AMT model that outperforms a recent strong baseline across five datasets, performs comparably to deep‑salience for MPE, uses harmonic stacking to stay low-resource, and achieves state-of-the-art results on GuitarSet.
supporting_quote: We demonstrate that the proposed low-resource neural network-based model (NMP) can be successfully applied to instrument-agnostic polyphonic note transcription and MPE. NMP outperforms a recent strong baseline note estimation model across five different datasets, and performs similarly to deep salience for MPE. Further, we see that the use of harmonic stacking allows our model to remain low-resource while maintaining its performance. When compared with instrument-specific models, we see that NMP achieves state-of-the-art results on GuitarSet.

learning: Spotify's Basic Pitch is presented as a polyphonic, instrument-agnostic audio→MIDI model that supports pitch-bend detection (vibrato/glissando/bends/slides) and is designed to be fast and lightweight.
source_title: Meet Basic Pitch: Spotify's Open Source Audio-to-MIDI Converter
supporting_quote:
While other note-detection systems have existed for years, Basic Pitch offers a number of advantages:

*   **Polyphonic + instrument-agnostic:** Unlike most other note-detection algorithms, Basic Pitch can track multiple notes at a time and across various instruments, including piano, guitar, and ocarina. Many systems limit users to only monophonic output (one note at a time, like a single vocal melody), or are built for only one kind of instrument.
    
*   **Pitch bend detection:** Instruments, like guitar or the human voice, allow for more expressiveness through pitch bending: vibrato, glissando, bends, slides, etc. However, this valuable information is often lost when turning audio into MIDI. Basic Pitch supports this right out of the box.
    
*   **Speed:** Basic Pitch is light on resources, and is able to run faster than real time on most modern computers (Bittner et al. 2022).

Goal: compile benchmark accuracy figures for polyphonic guitar transcription, onset detection, and tablature extraction on standard MIR datasets (GuitarSet, IRMAS where relevant, MusicNet, MAPS, and Spotify Basic Pitch/Pop datasets). Focus on reported metrics such as note F‑measure, onset/offset F1, onset tolerance windows, pitch‑class accuracy, transcription frame F1, and tablature/string/fret accuracy; include conditions that simulate realistic practice settings (backing‑track bleed, SNR levels, smartphone recordings, compression). Extract model types evaluated (classical signal processing, NMF, CRNN, Transformer, Basic Pitch/Onsets and Frames extensions), training data, and any reported degradation under noise/bleed (quantify performance drop per SNR or bleed percentage).

How to advance research after obtaining results: (1) Create a transparent benchmark table showing best‑reported numbers and experimental conditions (dataset split, polyphony, mixed‑audio bleed, mic type). (2) Define standardized robustness tests: SNR sweep (e.g., +20 to -10 dB), simulated backing‑track bleed levels, MP3/AAC compression, room reverberation; report metric decay curves so practitioners can anticipate real‑world performance. (3) Produce an error taxonomy for guitar transcription (missed fretted-note detection due to bending/vibrato, note splitting from distortion, false positives from backing tracks, string misassignment in tablature) and map these to downstream assessment risks (e.g., rhythm score misestimation vs. pitch‑based expressiveness misclassification). (4) Recommend augmentation/finetuning strategies (mixing dry guitar with real backing tracks, adversarial bleed examples, multi‑mic training) and evaluation protocols (holdout recordings recorded on smartphones/USB interfaces to measure generalization).

Additional directions: investigate how transcription uncertainty propagates into automated assessment metrics (propagate note onset/pitch confidence into score CIs), explore hybrid approaches using multi‑modal inputs (audio+video for fingering detection) to improve tablature extraction, and propose community benchmarks for ‘practice‑condition’ transcription with a shared corpus of smartphone recordings and backing tracks. Consider evaluation of Spotify Basic Pitch extensions and replicate top results with public code to verify reproducibility; where gaps exist, recommend replication studies under varied recording conditions.
